title: Vote share cutoff and policy adoption

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) exploiting the deterministic rule that an initiative is adopted if and only if its vote share is at least 50 %.  

Key identifying assumption (continuity): In the absence of adoption, expected municipal‐spending changes would evolve smoothly with the vote share in a narrow window around the 0.50 threshold. Any discontinuous jump in y at the cutoff can therefore be causally attributed to adoption.

## 2. R Code
```r
#################################################################
#  Sharp RDD: ballot‐initiative adoption and municipal spending #
#################################################################

# 1. Packages ---------------------------------------------------
need  <- c("rdrobust", "readr", "dplyr")
inst  <- need[!(need %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(inst)) install.packages(inst, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
lapply(need, library, character.only = TRUE)

# 2. Read data --------------------------------------------------
file_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s25_data.csv"
df <- read_csv(file_path, col_types = cols())

# 3. Center running variable at the cutoff ---------------------
df <- df %>% mutate(x = running_var - 0.5)   # x = 0 at the 50 % line

# 4. Main RDD estimate (local linear, MSE-optimal bandwidth) ---
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$x, c = 0)

cat("\n===== Main RDD estimate (full sample, h* from rdrobust) =====\n")
print(summary(rd_main))
cat("\nPoint estimate (tau_hat):", rd_main$coef[1], 
    "\nRobust SE:", rd_main$se[1], "\n")

# 5. Robustness check 1: pre-specified bandwidth (|x| ≤ 0.30) --
df_nc  <- df %>% filter(abs(x) <= 0.30)
rd_nc  <- rdrobust(y = df_nc$y, x = df_nc$x, c = 0, h = 0.30)

cat("\n===== Robustness: manual bandwidth 0.30 =====\n")
cat("tau_hat:", rd_nc$coef[1], " | Robust SE:", rd_nc$se[1], "\n")

# 6. Robustness check 2: half & double MSE bandwidths ----------
h_opt  <- rd_main$bws[1,1]
rd_h05 <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$x, c = 0, h = 0.5*h_opt)
rd_h20 <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$x, c = 0, h = 2*h_opt)

cat("\n===== Robustness: half and double bandwidths =====\n")
cat("Half h*:  tau_hat =", rd_h05$coef[1], " | SE =", rd_h05$se[1], "\n")
cat("Double h*:tau_hat =", rd_h20$coef[1], " | SE =", rd_h20$se[1], "\n")

# 7. Robustness check 3: quadratic control function ------------
quad_lm <- lm(y ~ treated + poly(x, 2), data = df_nc)
cat("\n===== Robustness: quadratic control function (|x|≤0.30) =====\n")
print(summary(quad_lm)$coefficients["treated",])

# 8. Clean numerical output (for easy extraction) --------------
cat("\n**************** SUMMARY ****************\n")
cat("Main RDD point estimate =", rd_main$coef[1], 
    "with robust SE =", rd_main$se[1], "\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Because adoption directs explicit resources to the policy area, we expect a positive discontinuity: municipalities whose initiatives barely pass should increase targeted spending relative to those that barely fail. Using log spending changes, a coefficient around +0.30 – 0.50 (≈ 35 %–65 % higher spending) would be economically plausible.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Sharp RDD — cutoff = 50% vote share; local linear regression with optimal bandwidth
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Passing the initiative causes a discrete jump in targeted spending
